Walkthrough: from weekly spend to a budget recommendation

Source: vignettes/articles/budget-walkthrough.Rmd
budget-walkthrough.Rmd

This article follows one question from raw data to an answer: if the marketing budget stays the same, should any of it move between channels? It uses the north geography of mm_weekly, 156 weeks of five channels, generated from known parameters so that every step can be checked against the truth.

The getting-started vignette, vignette("mediamix"), introduces each function. This article is about using them together, and about where the answer is solid and where it is not.

The setup keeps the parameters mm_weekly was generated from in truth, and adds a week counter to serve as the trend control:

library(mediamix)
data(mm_weekly)

channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")
north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
north <- north[order(north$date), ]
north$week <- seq_len(nrow(north))

1. Check the data can answer the question

A model can only tell channels apart if they move independently of one another and vary from week to week. diagnose_media() checks both before anything is fitted:

d <- diagnose_media(north, media = channels, decay = 0.6)
d
#> 
#> ── Media diagnostics
#> 156 observations across 1 series, 5 channels
#> Collinearity measured on adstocked media.
#> Ungrouped. On panel data, pass `by` so that collinearity is measured within
#> series.
#> ✔ No structural problems found.
#> 
#> Inspect $variation, $collinearity, $correlations.
d$collinearity[, c("channel", "vif", "most_correlated_with", "correlation")]
#>   channel   vif most_correlated_with correlation
#> 1  search 1.188                   tv      0.3173
#> 2      tv 1.176               search      0.3173
#> 3  social 1.169              display      0.2801
#> 4 display 1.148               social      0.2801
#> 5   video 1.076              display      0.1451

decay = 0.6 measures collinearity after a representative adstock, since smoothed series correlate more than raw spend and the model sees the smoothed ones. No channel is collinear enough to make its coefficient meaningless: the largest variance inflation factor (vif) is 1.19, well under diagnose_media()’s default warning level of 5. Every channel varies, but video and display are dark, with no spend at all, in 37% and 33% of weeks, so they carry less information than their row count suggests, which is worth remembering when their numbers come out.

2. Carryover: how well does the data identify it?

Tune every channel’s carryover at once, in one model that also holds the controls, so no channel is credited with another’s effect or with the trend:

controls <- north[c("week", "price", "seasonality", "holiday")]
grid <- seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05)

joint <- tune_carryover_joint(north[channels], north$revenue,
                              controls = controls, decays = grid)
rbind(truth  = truth$decay[channels],
      best   = joint$best$decay,
      one_se = joint$best_1se$decay)
#>          tv video search social display
#> truth  0.85  0.70   0.15   0.45    0.55
#> best   0.80  0.50   0.65   0.55    0.60
#> one_se 0.60  0.35   0.05   0.05    0.05

best is the minimum of each channel’s cross-validation curve, and one_se the shortest carryover within one standard error of it. The curves themselves show how firmly the data pins each decay down:

plot(joint, truth = truth$decay)

Television, social and display land within 0.1 of the truth and video within 0.2. Search does not, and its profile says why: it is nearly flat, so the data holds almost no information about search’s carryover. For search the one-standard-error choice falls back to a short carryover, which here is close to right; for every other channel it is shorter than the truth.

The joint search does not tune saturation. To keep this walkthrough about the decision rather than the estimation, the rest of it uses the generating parameters, which is what a full joint search over carryover and saturation, as in vignette("tidymodels"), is trying to reach. Section 7 comes back to what happens when television’s carryover is uncertain.

3. Fit the model

The model is ordinary least squares on the transformed media and the controls. spec holds each channel’s carryover and saturation. transform_plan() applies them to any spend plan and returns the plan with each channel’s column transformed, so section 7 can reuse spec on budgets that were never run:

spec <- lapply(channels, function(ch) list(
  adstock = list(decay = truth$decay[[ch]]),
  saturation = list(half_max = truth$half_max[[ch]],
                    shape = truth$shape[[ch]])
))
names(spec) <- channels

media <- transform_plan(north, spec)[channels]
model_data <- cbind(media, controls)
fit <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = model_data)
round(rbind(estimate = coef(fit)[channels], truth = truth$beta[channels]))
#>            tv video search social display
#> estimate 6013  1885   2622   2258     760
#> truth    5200  2400   4100   1800     900

Even with the transforms right, the coefficients land well away from the truth: search’s is 36% too low and social’s 25% too high. That is three years of weekly noise, and section 8 shows what it does to the answer.

4. Where did the revenue come from?

contributions() splits each week’s fitted revenue into one part per channel and a baseline, and roi() divides each channel’s total contribution by its total spend to give its average return:

contrib <- contributions(media, fit, index = north$date)
avg <- roi(contrib, north[channels])
avg
#>   channel contribution  spend   roi
#> 1  social       132709  36716 3.614
#> 2  search       208307  74560 2.794
#> 3   video       102461  53248 1.924
#> 4 display        40853  26937 1.517
#> 5      tv       349629 266978 1.310

Every channel returns more than it costs on average. On this table alone the tempting move is to take money from television, the lowest average ROI, and give it to social, the highest.

5. What would the next pound do?

Average ROI describes the budget that was spent. The reallocation question is about the margin, and marginal_roi() answers it by re-running the whole transform on a slightly larger budget. Given the plan, the coefficients and spec, it does every channel at once, and its roi column is the average return from section 4:

marginal <- marginal_roi(north, coef(fit), spec = spec)
marginal[order(-marginal$mroi), c("channel", "mroi", "roi", "spend")]
#>   channel   mroi   roi  spend
#> 4  social 2.0892 3.614  36716
#> 3  search 1.3490 2.794  74560
#> 1      tv 1.2534 1.310 266978
#> 2   video 1.1961 1.924  53248
#> 5 display 0.9324 1.517  26937

The ranking changes. Social still has the highest marginal return, but television is no longer at the bottom: its S-shaped response means its next pound works nearly as hard as its average one. Display is now last, and its estimated marginal return is below 1: in this model, the last pounds spent on it did not pay for themselves.

The chart sets each channel’s average return (open circle) beside its marginal return (filled circle); the vertical line is break-even:

So in this model the candidate move is display to social, not television to social.

6. How sure are we?

Every number so far is a point estimate from one sample of 156 weeks. A block bootstrap resamples runs of consecutive weeks, refits the model, and recomputes, which shows how much of the ranking survives sampling noise. The transform is not re-run on the resampled rows, because that would glue unrelated weeks together and carry spend across the joins. Each replicate refits the coefficients on resampled rows and recomputes average and marginal return on the original spend plan:

boot_data <- cbind(revenue = north$revenue, media, controls)

returns <- function(d) {
  f <- lm(revenue ~ ., data = d)
  r <- marginal_roi(north, coef(f), spec = spec)
  out <- c(rbind(r$roi, r$mroi))
  names(out) <- paste(rep(r$channel, each = 2), c("average", "marginal"),
                      sep = ": ")
  out
}

boot <- block_bootstrap(boot_data, returns, times = 200, block_length = 13,
                        seed = 2026)
boot
#> 
#> ── Block bootstrap
#> 200 replicates, blocks of 13 rows, 90% percentile intervals
#>               term estimate   lower upper std_error
#>        tv: average   1.3096  1.0698 1.664    0.1924
#>       tv: marginal   1.2534  1.0240 1.592    0.1842
#>     video: average   1.9242  0.3211 3.291    0.9783
#>    video: marginal   1.1961  0.1996 2.046    0.6081
#>    search: average   2.7938  1.1118 4.545    1.0664
#>   search: marginal   1.3490  0.5368 2.194    0.5149
#>    social: average   3.6145  0.9283 4.900    1.2335
#>   social: marginal   2.0892  0.5365 2.832    0.7130
#>   display: average   1.5166 -0.5923 4.358    1.5145
#>  display: marginal   0.9324 -0.3642 2.679    0.9311
plot(boot, reference = 1, xlab = "Revenue per pound")

The intervals are wide. Only the intervals for tv: average, tv: marginal and search: average lie entirely above break-even; every other interval crosses 1, and both of display’s reach below zero. They hold the transforms at the true parameters chosen in section 3, so they show sampling uncertainty in the coefficients only. Two channels’ intervals overlapping does not settle a comparison between them, because their estimates move together from replicate to replicate, so ask the paired question directly:

reps <- attr(boot, "replicates")
paired <- c(social_beats_display = mean(reps[, "social: marginal"] >
                                          reps[, "display: marginal"]),
            social_beats_tv      = mean(reps[, "social: marginal"] >
                                          reps[, "tv: marginal"]))
paired
#> social_beats_display      social_beats_tv 
#>                 0.72                 0.80

Social’s marginal return beats display’s in 72% of replicates and television’s in 80%. That is the honest strength of the evidence for moving money into social: more likely right than wrong, and not more than that. It is a reason to run the move as a test, not to announce it.

7. Test the move before recommending it

A marginal return is a derivative. A real reallocation is a finite change, and the response curves bend along the way, so simulate the new plan through the model rather than multiplying by a marginal rate. reallocate() builds the new plan, keeping each channel’s flighting: it takes the amount from one channel in proportion to its spend in each week and adds it to the other in proportion to that channel’s. simulate_plan() runs a plan through spec and the coefficients, and with baseline it adds each channel’s change in spend and in predicted response. Everything except the two channels is held fixed, and the controls do not change, so the sum of response_change is the difference in predicted revenue:

tenth <- 0.10 * sum(north$display)
to_social <- reallocate(north, from = "display", to = "social",
                        amount = tenth)
simulate_plan(to_social, spec, coef(fit), baseline = north)
#>   channel  spend response spend_change response_change
#> 1      tv 266978   349629            0               0
#> 2   video  53248   102461            0               0
#> 3  search  74560   208307            0               0
#> 4  social  39410   138198         2694            5489
#> 5 display  24243    38235        -2694           -2618

The same two steps compare several moves, here by the gain per pound moved:

move <- function(from, to, amount, spec, coefficients = coef(fit)) {
  plan <- reallocate(north, from = from, to = to, amount = amount)
  change <- simulate_plan(plan, spec, coefficients, baseline = north)
  gain <- sum(change$response_change)
  c(moved = amount, revenue_change = gain, per_pound_moved = gain / amount)
}

rbind(
  `display -> social` = move("display", "social", tenth, spec),
  `tv -> social`      = move("tv", "social", tenth, spec),
  `display -> social, 2.5x` = move("display", "social", 2.5 * tenth, spec)
)
#>                         moved revenue_change per_pound_moved
#> display -> social        2694           2871          1.0659
#> tv -> social             2694           2090          0.7760
#> display -> social, 2.5x  6734           6213          0.9226

In the model, moving a tenth of display’s budget into social raises predicted revenue at no extra cost. Moving the same amount out of television instead, the move the average-ROI table suggested, gains less, because it gives up television’s still-steep fitted response. Moving two and a half times as much out of display gains more in total but less per pound, as social climbs its own curve.

Two checks before this goes in a deck. First, is the new plan inside the data?

peak <- function(amount) {
  max(reallocate(north, from = "display", to = "social",
                 amount = amount)$social)
}
c(observed = max(north$social), smaller_move = peak(tenth),
  larger_move = peak(2.5 * tenth))
#>     observed smaller_move  larger_move 
#>        652.0        699.8        771.6

Both moves push social’s busiest week above anything in the data: the smaller by about 7%, the larger by about 18%. A little beyond the observed range is the unavoidable price of asking what more would do, but the further out a plan goes, the more of its predicted gain is the fitted curve’s shape rather than evidence. The smaller move stays close enough to the data to be worth testing; the larger one should wait for that test.

Second, how sensitive is the answer to carryover it could not pin down? In section 2 the data was consistent with a television decay as low as the one-standard-error value. Refit with that, and compare television’s marginal return and the display-to-social move under the two fits:

tv_alt <- joint$best_1se$decay[joint$best_1se$channel == "tv"]
spec_alt <- spec
spec_alt$tv$adstock$decay <- tv_alt

media_alt <- transform_plan(north, spec_alt)[channels]
fit_alt <- lm(north$revenue ~ ., data = cbind(media_alt, controls))

tv_mroi_alt <- marginal_roi(north, coef(fit_alt), spec = spec_alt["tv"])$mroi
sensitivity <- rbind(
  true_decay   = c(tv_decay = truth$decay[["tv"]],
                   tv_mroi = marginal$mroi[marginal$channel == "tv"],
                   display_to_social = move("display", "social", tenth,
                                            spec)[["per_pound_moved"]]),
  one_se_decay = c(tv_decay = tv_alt,
                   tv_mroi = tv_mroi_alt,
                   display_to_social = move("display", "social", tenth, spec_alt,
                                            coef(fit_alt))[["per_pound_moved"]])
)
sensitivity
#>              tv_decay tv_mroi display_to_social
#> true_decay       0.85  1.2534            1.0659
#> one_se_decay     0.60  0.7886            0.2671

Television’s marginal return depends heavily on a carryover the data only loosely identifies: at the shorter decay its next pound no longer pays for itself. The display-to-social move does not touch television’s budget, but it is not immune either, because refitting moves display’s and social’s coefficients too: it still gains, but 0.27 per pound moved rather than 1.07. Its direction survives a carryover the data cannot rule out, which makes it the cleaner test; its size does not. Whether television is over- or under-funded is a question this data cannot settle, and saying so is part of the answer.

The moves so far were chosen by hand. allocate_budget() asks what the fitted model would do with the whole budget: how to split the same total across all five channels so that predicted media response is as large as possible.

best <- allocate_budget(north, spec, coef(fit))
best$allocation[, c("channel", "current_spend", "recommended_spend", "mroi")]
#>   channel current_spend recommended_spend  mroi
#> 1      tv        266978            254434 1.292
#> 2   video         53248             48136 1.285
#> 3  search         74560             77935 1.289
#> 4  social         36716             61889 1.297
#> 5 display         26937             16045 1.297
plot(best)

It rescales each channel’s whole series, so every channel keeps its flighting and only its total changes. It works out each channel’s predicted response at every multiple of a step, here 2,292, and picks the combination that spends the whole budget with the largest predicted response. On the fitted model that takes money from television, video and display and puts most of it into social. At the recommended split the channels’ marginal returns all lie between 1.29 and 1.30, against 0.93 to 2.09 now.

The allocation works from point estimates. It takes the coefficients and spec as exact, so read it together with section 6, where social’s marginal return beat display’s in 72% of replicates and television’s in 80%, and with the carryover check above: it cuts television, the channel that check could not call either way. It also goes where the data does not, raising social’s busiest week to 1,099, 69% above anything observed. It is the fitted model’s best split on that grid, and, like the moves above, a hypothesis to test.

8. Check the answer against the truth

mm_weekly was simulated, so this decision can be checked against the parameters that generated it, which a real analysis never can. The same marginal returns and moves, with the true coefficients in place of the fitted ones:

true_returns <- marginal_roi(north, truth$beta, spec = spec)
true_mroi <- stats::setNames(true_returns$mroi, true_returns$channel)
round(rbind(fitted = stats::setNames(marginal$mroi, marginal$channel),
            truth = true_mroi), 2)
#>          tv video search social display
#> fitted 1.25  1.20   1.35   2.09    0.93
#> truth  1.08  1.52   2.11   1.67    1.10

true_per_pound <- function(from, to, amount) {
  move(from, to, amount, spec, truth$beta)[["per_pound_moved"]]
}
true_moves <- c(`display -> social` = true_per_pound("display", "social", tenth),
                `tv -> social`      = true_per_pound("tv", "social", tenth),
                `tv -> search`      = true_per_pound("tv", "search", tenth))
round(true_moves, 2)
#> display -> social      tv -> social      tv -> search 
#>              0.47              0.53              0.99

# The allocation from section 7, and the best split under the truth
best_true <- allocate_budget(north, spec, truth$beta)
gain <- function(allocation, coefficients) {
  sum(simulate_plan(allocation$plan, spec, coefficients,
                    baseline = north)$response_change)
}
allocation_gain <- c(predicted = gain(best, coef(fit)),
                     in_truth = gain(best, truth$beta),
                     best_in_truth = gain(best_true, truth$beta))
round(allocation_gain)
#>     predicted      in_truth best_in_truth 
#>         11642          3942         27020

The direction of the display-to-social move holds up: it raises revenue in truth too. Everything else this analysis concluded about the ranking does not. The fitted model overstates that move’s gain per pound about 2.3-fold, and in truth television has the lowest marginal return (1.08) and search the highest (2.11), so the best move takes from television, the channel this analysis could not call either way, and gives to search. The allocation fares the same way. Its split still gains in truth, but 3,942 rather than the 11,642 the fitted model predicted, while the split that is best under the true parameters would gain 27,020.

No step above was a mistake of method. Three years of weekly noise moved the coefficients enough to reorder channels whose true returns sit within a few tenths of each other, which is what the wide intervals in section 6 and the 72% paired probability were saying. A real analysis has no truth to check against, which is why the next section treats the result as a hypothesis.

9. What to say, and what not to

The analysis supports a test, not a reallocation. The fitted model points at moving around a tenth of display’s budget into social; the bootstrap puts the odds of that ranking at roughly 72 in 100; and section 8 shows how a fitted model can misrank channels whose returns are close. Run the move as a geo experiment: change the allocation in one region, compare it with the others, and use the measured result to calibrate the model’s priors or constraints. Leave television’s budget alone until its carryover is better measured, in either direction.

reallocate() sets up the test plan: with by = "geo" and an amount named by region, it moves spend in that region only.

test_plan <- reallocate(mm_weekly, from = "display", to = "social",
                        amount = c(north = tenth), by = "geo")
tapply(test_plan$social - mm_weekly$social, mm_weekly$geo, sum)
#> central   north   south 
#>       0    2694       0

What this analysis does not support: a precise revenue forecast for the new plan, any move that takes a channel far outside the spend it has historically run at, or a ranking of channels by average ROI, or by marginal ROI without a test.
